description_full: Lincoln Educational Services Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, provides various career-oriented postsecondary education services to high school graduates and working adults in the United States. It operates in two segments, Campus Operations and Transitional. The company offers associate's degree, and diploma and certificate programs in automotive technology; skilled trades programs, including electrical, heating and air conditioning repair, welding, computerized numerical control, and electrical and electronic systems technology; and health science and information technology programs. It operates schools under the Lincoln Technical Institute, Lincoln College of Technology, and Nashville Auto Diesel College brands. Lincoln Educational Services Corporation was founded in 1946 and is headquartered in Parsippany, New Jersey.

financial_summary: Lincoln Educational Services Co is a small-cap consumer defensive business with a $702M market cap on $518M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +14% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 19% against a 10% cost of capital — a 9-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.
The company is burning through $27M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 8.9×.
Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 7.4% of the shares.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).

Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+11.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 13% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 24% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 60% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 60% and a beta of 1.07, it moves roughly with the market.
About $17.6M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.5x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 40% in the 2020 crash, 39% in the 2022 bear market and 31% in 2008.
val: On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 30.0 vs 18.3 and EV/EBITDA 14.1 vs 10.2 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 72% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of -3.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 5 covering analysts target $39.40 on average, 73% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 19% clears the cost of capital of 9.9% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.78).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.97x.
ROE of 10% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.1% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
The current ratio of 0.86 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 14.2% over 3 years, 12.1% over 5 years and 10.4% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 18%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 19.2% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs 4.5x depreciation (16.7% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 6, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 7.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 95%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (16 sales, net $15.5M sold).
The share count has grown 2.7% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
